caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 48 of 1989.
lawyer:
Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. H. R. Sharif with Mr. Shima Jahur, Advocates ----- For the Appellants.
Mr. Mahmudul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No. 1. 
Mr. Zakir Hossain, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Silver Estate Ltd ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Hakim Mia and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 18.2.1989 passed by the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 29 of 1983 dismissing the suit for Specific Performance of Contract for sale of the suit property after declaring that the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 have no right, title and interest therein.

2. The appellant as plaintiff filed the aforesaid Title Suit No. 29 of 1983 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the respondents as defendants alleging inter alia that the suit property being plot No. 6 Delkusha Commercial Area, Dhaka measuring an area of 10(ten) kathas, 1(one) chatak, 27 (twenty seven) Sft. was leased out by the defendant No. 5, Dhaka Improvement Trust to Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works of 7, BK Das Road, Dhaka by a registered deed of lease dated 13.12.67 for 99 years; that the said Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works with permission of the Dhaka Improvement Trust dated 13.3.1973 transferred the suit plot to M/s. Hakim Humayun and Company represented by its proprietor, Abdul Hakim Miah, defendant No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 27.6.73 with delivery of possession to the said transferee; thereafter the defendant No. 1 constructed a one storied building in the suit plot after obtaining approved plan for a ten storied building. The defendant No. 1 entered into a written agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property at a consideration of Tk. 43,000.00 and received the sum of Tk. 3,00,000.00 as earnest money on 15.7.82 on executing the said agreement; that in pursuance of the said agreement the defendant No. 1 applied to the DIT for permission to transfer the suit property to the plaintiff and by Memo dated 19.8.82 the DIT directed to deposit transfer fee of Tk. 5,05,000.00 plus Tk. 909.00 as service charge; defendant No. 2 published notice in the newspapers and also sent notice through his Advocate to the plaintiff claiming that the suit property belonged to the firm M/S. Hakim Humayun and Co. of which he was a partner to the extent of 50% and the defendant No. 4 to the extent of remaining 50%; that the plaintiff further learnt that the defendant No. 2 had filed Title Suit No. 417 of 1982 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against defendant No. 1 for declaration that he was the owner of 8.00 annas share of the suit property and that the Memo dated 19.8.82 issued by the DIT directing defendant No. 1 to deposit transfer fee etc. was illegal and had obtained an order of status-quo in that suit; that the plaintiff further learnt that the defendant No. 1 had filed Title Suit No. 771 of 1979 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for partition of ejmali properties including the suit property; that the defendant No. 1 is the owner of the suit property but he has been refusing to perform his obligations under the contract for sale in collusion with/the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 to frustrate the contract though they have no title in the suit property; Title Suit No. 771 of 1979 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and Title suit No. 417 of 1982 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka are collusive proceedings between the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 and inspire of statements made in those suits the defendant No. 1 remained owner of the suit property and those suits were collusive and instituted only to defeat the interest of the plaintiff. The cause of action for the suit arose on 15.7.82 when contract for sale was made and then on 4.9.82 when notice was served on the plaintiff by the defendant No. 2 through his Advocate and on 2.1.83 when defendant No. 1 refused to enforce the contract.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 5 by filing separate written statements.

4. The defendant No. 1 denied most of the allegations made in the plaint in his written statement and admitted that the defendant No. 1 is the sole owner of the suit property as proprietor of M/S. Hakim Humayun and Co. and also admitted the contract dated 15.7.82 for sate of the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of Tk. 43,00,000.00 and payment of Tk. 3,00,000.00 as advance and also admitted that on the application of the defendant No. 1 for permission to transfer the suit property DIT by Memo dated 19.8.82 directed him to deposit Tk. 5,05,000.00 as transfer fee plus Tk. 909.00 as service charge. The defendant No. 1 asserted that on the next date he made over the said letter to the plaintiff to pay the said amounts to the DIT in terms of the contract with him at an early date for getting transfer permission but the plaintiff deliberately delayed the matter as he had not the requisite fund to deposit the transfer fee and service charges and the plaintiff caused service of the alleged legal notice by the defendant No. 2 in collusion with him and also managed to publish notices by defendant No. 2 in the newspapers. It was due to the plaintiffs failure to perform his part of the contract that the sale deed could not be executed and registered. The plaintiff got Title Suit No. 417 of 1982 filed by the defendant No. 2 and obtained order of status-quo against defendant No. 1 for delaying the matter. The plaintiff was fully aware of the permission accorded by the DIT for transfer and was fully satisfied as to the right of the defendant No. 1 in respect of the suit property and there was no reason for him to be influenced by the defendant 2. It showed that the plaintiff had not the means to pay the price of the suit property and adopted the double role. The claim of defendant No. 2 in Title Suit No. 417 of 1982 was absolutely false and baseless. Title Suit No. 771 of 1979 was a collusive suit for partition which was fraudulently managed to be filed by the defendant No. 2 by misrepresentation and fraud and suit property was fraudulently inserted in the schedule of that plaint and when it came to the light the matter was attempted to be compromised out of Court and a petition of withdrawal of the suit was filed on 15.9.1981 and as such the suit was not in existence in the eye of law on the date of filing Title Suit No. 417 of 1982 by the defendant No. 2. The defendant never avoided or refused to perform his part of the contract and he had always been earnest to perform his part of the contract and he was never in collusion with defendant Nos. 2 and 4 but the plaintiff made inordinate delay to pay the transfer fee and service charge and due to plaintiffs delay the purpose for sale to invest money for which the defendant No. 1 entered into the contract to sell the suit property was frustrated. Since the plaintiff avoided his obligations under the contract he was not entitled to the prayer for decree and the suit was liable to be dismissed.

5. The defendant No. 5 also contested the suit by filing another written statement contending, inter alia that no notice under the provision of Town Improvement Act was serviced upon the defendant before filing the suit and as such the suit was not maintainable against defendant No. 5; that the defendant No. 1 as the sole sixteen annas owner of M/S. Hakim Humayun and Co. prayed for permission from DIT to transfer the suit plot to the plaintiff and by Memo dated 19.8.82 DIT directed the allottee to deposit transfer fee of Tk. 5,05,000.00 and service charge of Tk. 909.00 but as the same were not paid transfer could not be finally effected and as such the suit was liable to be dismissed.

6. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by filing another separate written statement contested the suit denying the material allegations and alleging inter alia that the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 are full brothers; that 'the defendant No. 4 used to reside at the village home and the defendant No. 2 started a business at 31, Bangshi Bazar, Dhaka for selling brass etc; that with the income of that business defendant No. 2 purchased land at Kadam Bagchar (Shyampur) and started metal works under the name of M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works; that thereafter defendant No. 2 brought his brothers from his village and constituted a partnership for establishing and running the factory; that subsequently the defendant No. 3 in 1963 applied to the DIT for allotment of a plot of land to M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works and on 11.12.67 defendant No. 5 allotted suit plot to M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works and on 13.12.67 executed and registered the lease deed, that defendant No. 4 in breach of trust reposed on him signed the lease deed as proprietor though M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works was a partnership concern; that defendant Nos. 2 and 4 started another partnership business under the name of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. and the defendant No. 4 in breach of the trust reposed upon him transferred the suit plot on behalf of M/S. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works to M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. showing defendant No. 1 as the proprietor though as a matter of fact defendant No. 1. was merely a paper proprietor of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. and only his name was tended in the transfer to avoid income tax and other complications; that possession was never handed over to defendant No. 1; that defendant Nos. 2 and 4 paid the fees and furnished the undertaking in the benami of defendant No. 1 but mutation was done in the name of defendant No. 3; that when fraud of defendant No. 4 was detected the firm was reconstituted with defendant Nos. 2 and 4; that previous partners Mrs. Azimunnessa, Md. Azizul Huq and Abdul Hakim Mia (defendant No. 1) retired from that firm by publishing public notice in the newspaper and the Registrar of Firms was given intimation of such retirement and reconstitution of the Firm; that defendant No. 4 as plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No. 1 as plaintiff No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 771 of 1979 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against defendant No. 2 and others for partition and in schedule 'D' of that plaint the suit property is shown with averments in para 12 of the plaint to the effect that Abdul Kader Mia and Abdul Wahed Mia were the two partners of MIS. Hakim Humayun and Co. each having 8 annas share and suit plot was transferred to the said firm by a registered deed of sale dated 27.6.73 with delivery of possession and the defendant No. 2 constructed one storied building thereon with ten storied foundation and the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 have equal shares of 8 annas each; that thereafter a compromise petition was drawn and signed by the parties admitting 8 annas share of the defendant No. 2 in the suit property as partner of defendant No. 3; that a family settlement deed was also executed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 and others on 7.10.81 admitting 8 annas share of defendant No. 2 in the properties of defendant No. 3 (the suit property); that on 20.7.82 the defendant No. 1 in conspiracy with defendant No. 4 filed an application to defendant No. 5 for permission to transfer the suit property falsely showing him as the sole proprietor of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. though defendant No. 1 was merely a name lender; that defendant No. 5 issued letter dated 19.8.82 directing defendant No. 1 to deposit transfer fee of Tk. 5,05,000.00 and service charge of Tk. 909.00 in an unauthorised manner for which the defendant No. 2 was compelled to file Title Suit No. 417 of 1982 which is pending; that the instant suit was a collusive proceeding between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 to grab the suit property; that the alleged contract is collusive, fraudulent, malafide and colourable without any consideration and to grab the suit property though defendant No. 1 has no right, title and interest in the suit property; that in a meeting on 6.3.83 at the Bar Library premises the defendant No. 1 admitted that the alleged contract was colourable and to put pressure on defendant No. 2 for compelling him to register kabalas pending in the Registration Officer and if the same were done by the defendant No. 2 and his sons then Motijheel property would be taken back from the plaintiff and Khondker Mahtabuddin agreed to the same; that the suit was liable to be dismissed and was not maintainable in the present from.

7. The following issues were framed in the suit :

1.	Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2.	Is the suit barred by limitation?

3.	Is the alleged contract between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 correct and true?

4.	Have the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 any right, title and possession in the suit property?

5.	Is the plaintiff entitled to any relief, if so, to what relief he is entitled ?

8. The plaintiff examined Khandker Mahtabuddin, its managing Director as PW 1, Tajul Islam Chowdhury an attesting witness of the deed of agreement as PW 2 and also produced and proved deed of agreement dated 15.7.82 as Ext. 1; Original lease deed Ext. 2, sale deed dated 27.6.73 Ext. 3, permission from DIT Ext. 4, copy of newspapers Exts. 5 and 5(a), legal notice Ext. 6, objection notice published in the newspaper Ext. 7, copy of the plaint of TS No. 133 of 1984 Ext. 8. The defendant No. 1 examined himself as DW 1 and produced and proved Import Registration Certificate Ext. 'Ka' (‘ক’) Newspaper Ext. Kha (‘খ’), Copy of petition dated 8.7.84 Ext. 'Ga' (‘গ’), copy of petition dated 9.12.84 Ext. 'Gha' (‘ঘ’); copy of order dated 19.12.84 in TS No. 771 of 1979 Ext. Uma (‘ঙ’).

9. The defendant No. 2 examined himself as DW 2, Amir Mia was examined as DW No. 3 Saizuddin as DW 4. Defendant No. 2 produced and proved deed of partnership dated 22.10.56 Ext. 2 Ka (2 ‘ক’), partnership registration certificate dated 11.10.62 Ext. 2 Kha (2 ‘খ’); Certificate copy of the deed of lease Ext. 2 Ga (2 ‘গ’); Partnership deed dated 25.4.77 Ext. 2 Gha (2‘ঘ’); Certificate of Registration of Firm Ext. 2 Uma (2 ‘ঙ’), Receipts granted by the Contractor who constructed the building in the suit plot Ext. 2 Cha (2‘চ’ ) series, Copy of the plaint of TS 771 of 1979 Ext. 2 Chha (2‘ছ’), copy of the legal notice by his Advocate to the plaintiff Ext. 2 Ja (2জ), copy of the letter of objection to DIT Ext. 2 Jha(2ঝ), copy of application to DIT for correction of mutation dated 30.8.82 Ext. 2 Niya (2), copy of order of status quo dated 6.9.82 passed in TS No. 417 of 1982 Ext. 2 Ta (2ট), copy of letter to DIT intimating about injunction order Ext. 2 Tha (2ঠ), deed of family settlement dated 7.10.81 Ext 2 Da (2ড), deed of sale dated 4.6.84 transferring interest of M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works in his favour Ext. 2 Tha (2ঢ), deed executed by Amin Mia in favour of defendant No. 2 Na (2ন), copy of deed dated 17.12.81 executed by Kader Mia in favour of defendant No. 2 Ext. 2 Ta (2ত), copies of 9 other deeds executed by Kader Mia regarding Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works Exts. 2 Ta(1) to 2 Ta(9), (2ত(১)) to (2ত(৯)), Deed of sale dated 18.2.65 in respect of 37/1, Dina NathSen Road Ext. 2 Tha (2থ), copy of attachment order in TS No. 12 of 1984 Ext. 2 Da (2দ).

10. On behalf of the defendant No. 5 Md. Abu Bakkar Sk. an Assistant Director of DIT at prese RAJUK deposed as DW 5. The said witness produced and proved application dated 16.3.62 filed by A Kader for allotment of a plot Ext 3 Ka (3K), Deed of lease dated 13.12.67 Ext 3 Kha (3L) allotment letter dated 31.5.62 Ext 3 Ga(3M) application dated 8.7.70 filed by A Kader for permission to sell the suit plot Ext 3 Gha (3N) copy of the letter dated 13.3.73 granting permission to transfer suit plot to M/s Hakim Humayun and Co. Ext 3 Uma (3O)certified copy of the transfer deed in favour of M/s Hakim Humayun and Co. Ext 3 Cha (3P); deed of agreement between A. Hakim on behalf of M/s Hakim Hamayun and Co Ext 3 Chha (3Q) copy of letter dated 3.9.73 intimating M/s Hakim Hamayun and Co about mutation of suit plot in the name of M/s Hakim Hamayun and Co. Ext 3 Ja (3R) application filed by M/s Hakim Humayan and Co. On 20.7.82 for permission to transfer suit property to plaintiff Ext 3 Jha(3S) copy of letter issued by RAJUK on 19.8.82 granting permission to transfer suit and Ext. 3 Niya (3T)

11. On consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary the Court below arrived at the following findings and conclusions:

1. That the suit is not barred by limitation.

2. That there was an agreement between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 to transfer the suit property.

3. Though the plaintiff did not deposit transfer fee and other charges in terms of the agreement dated 15.7.82 after permission from the DIT it could not be said that the plaintiff violated the terms of the agreement with the defendant No. 1.

4. Though Abdul Kader Mia signed the deed of lease dated dated 13.12.67 in respect of the suit land as proprietor of M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works, the said business concern was a partnership firm as per deed dated 22.10.56 and Abdul Kader Mia as Managing partner of the said firm filed application on 8.7.70 to DIT seeking permission to transfer the suit property to M/s Hakim Humayun and Co.

5. Though defendant No. 1 claimed himself as proprietor of M/s Hakim Humayun it appears from registered deed dated 25.4.77 that Abdul Kader Mia and Abdul Washed Mia are partners in equal shares of the said business concern.

6. There is dispute over title of the suit property between defendant nos 1 and 2 and the same is pending in court and defendant No. 1 has no right to transfer the suit property alone.

7. The dispute of title between the defendant nos 1 and 2 over the suit property can not be legally decided in the present suit brought by the plaintiff.

8. Plaintiff's suit for specific performance of contract for sale of suit land against defendant No. 1 and for declaration that defendant Nos 2 and 4 have not title therein is not maintainable as plaintiff has no locus standi to file such a suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, since the agreement for sale did not create any interest in the suit property.

9. The plaintiff is not legally entitled to any relief in the present suit.

12. Mr. HR Sharif; learned Advocate for the appellant after placing the pleadings, depositions, decoments and judgment of the court below made the following submissions:

That the Court below having found that there was contract for sale of the suit property by the defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiff and that the plaintiff did not violate any term of the said contract was wholly wrong in not passing a decree for specific performance of the the said contract for sale on an erroneous view that there was dispute of title between the dependent Nos 1 and 2 and the defendant No. 1 has no right alone to transfer the suit property. He further submitted that the Court below having found that the suit property was sold by the original allottee and lessee M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works to M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. represented by its sole proprietor Abdul Hakim, the defendant No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 27.6.73 (Ext. 3) with due permission from the DIT defendant No. 5, subsequent partnership between defendants Nos. 2 and 4 by registered deed dated 25.4.77 (Ext. 2 ga) could not confer title of the suit property to the defendant Nos. 2 and 4 as partners of M/s. Hakim Hamayun and Co since M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co as a prorietory concern represented by the defendant No. 1 as sole proprietor did not transfer interest in the suit property to the subsequently created partnership firm M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. represented by partners defendant Nos. 2 and 4 by a registered deed of transfer.

13. Learned Advocate further submitted that since in paragraph No. 6 of the plaint the plaintiff asserted that the suit property was transferred to M/s Hakim Humayun and Co. represented by its proprietor defendant No. 1 vide sale deed dated 27.6.73 in reply to the same the defendant Nos 2 and 3 in paragraph No 12 and 13 of their written statement averred that the defendant No. 1 was a mere paper proprietor of the firm M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. and only his name was lended in the transfer from M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works to avoid income tax and other complications and that deft No. 1 was a mere benamdar of deft Nos 2 and 4 and since deft Nos 2 and 3 did not adduce any evidence to discharge the onus to show that the defendant No. 1 was a mere paper proprietor of the firm M/s Hakim Humuyun and Co and was a mere name lender the Court below erred in not holding that the defendant No. 1 was the owner and as such he had absolute right to transfer the suit property in terms of the agreement of sale dated 15.7.82 as defendant No. 5 as lessor granted permission to him to transfer the suit property.

14. Mr. Khandkar Mahbabuddin Ahmed, the learned Sr. Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submitted that the court below erred in holding that the suit was not maintainable. The two reliefs prayed for in the suit one for specific performance of contract for sale of the shit property and the other for declaration that defendant Nos. 2 and 4 have no right, title and interest in the suit property are severable and prayer for specific performance of contract ought to have been decreed when the contract between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 was proved. He further submitted that even if the contention of defendant No. 2 that defendant No. 1 was mere name lender and benamdar was accepted there was no difficulty in passing a decree for specific performance of contract since under the provision of Section 41 Transfer of Property Act an ostensible owner can sell the property and that will not affect interest of the defendant No. 2 and the question whether defendant No. 1 was benamdar or real owner could be decided subsequently between the plaintiff and defendant No. 2. He lastly submitted that the court below erred in law in not passing a decree for refund of the sum of Taka 3,00,000.00 advanced by the plaintiff to the defendant No. 1 with compensation.

15. Mr. Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2 submitted that relief of specific performance of contract was discretionary and the Court is not bound to grant such a relief merely because the contract has been proved and the Court below rightly dismissed the suit on a clear finding that title of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property was in serious dispute in two previously instituted pending suits between the defendants. When a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of landed property is decreed on the failure of the defendant to amicably execute and register the sale deed and deliver possession the court is to do the same on behalf of the defendant in execution of the decree for specific performance of contract and when there is dispute of title over such property it will not be just and proper on the part of the Court to oust a third party from his possession. Faced with such circumstances the court below rightly refused to exercise its desecretion by dismissing the suit. He further submitted that in view of the admission of the defendant No. 1 made in the plaint of TS No. 771/1979 and family settlement deed dated 7.10.1981 that the suit property belonged to the partnership firm M/s Hakim Hamayun and Co. of which defendant Nos 2 and 4 were the only partners and as such the suit property belonged to them, the agreement dated 15.7.82 for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 was fraudulent and collusive transaction and the instant suit was a clear device to pre-empt the decision in their favour and to avoid the two pending suits between the defendants.

16. He further submitted that the defendant No. 2 has proved by oral as well as documentary evidence that M/s Hakim Humayun and Co was a partnership firm onus shifted on the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 to show that the same was a proprietory concern and they failed to discharge the said onus. Certificate dated 18.4.77 by the Registcrar of Firms was conclusive evidence u/s 68 Partnership Act that the said firm M/s Hakim Humayun and Co was reconstituted with defendant Nos 2 and 4 after retirement of other partners including defendant No. 1 Since the defendant No. 2 raised objection asserting title in the suit property provision of transfer by a benamdar under the provision of section 41 Transfer of Property Act was not applicable in the facts and circumstance of the case. Since the plaintiff has not come with clean hands he is not entitled to equitable relief by way of specific performance of contract.

17. Mr. Mahumudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 submitted that there was no breach of contract by the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff failed to prove the same. The plaintiff ought to have elected before filing the suit either to pray for specific performance of contract against defendant No. 1 if there was any breach on the part of defendant No. 1 or to sue all the defendants with additional prayer for declaration as has been done in this suit but at this stage the plaintiff cannot be allowed to abandon the prayer for declaration when the court refused to grant specific performance. He further submitted that if the contract is enforced against defendant No. 1 his client would be seriously prejudiced since value of money has depreciated very much. Had the plaintiff paid the entire consideration money in terms of the contract defendant No. 1 could have invested the amount in business or bank and it would have been more than doubled in the meantime. But the plaintiff without performing his part of the contract rushed to the court only with the malafide motive of delaying the matter as he was not in a position to deposit the transfer fee and balance of the consideration. He further submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case plaintiff appellant was entitled to refund of the earnest money from defendant No. 1 and since there was no breach of contract nor refusal to refund the earnest money the plaintiff was not entitled to compensation or interest. In support of his contentions he referred to the decisions reported in AIR 1915 Mad 305 PLD 1947 PC 407 and also sections 19 and 22 of the Specific Relief Act.

18. Learned Advocate for the appellant in reply referred to the decisions reported in 52 IC 971 AIR 1926 Mad 579, AIR 1961 Raj 196 and AIR 1943 Mad 497 in support of the contention that in a suit for specific performance of contract court can decide dispute of title and a prayer for declaration at the instance of such plaintiff was maintainable. The learned Advocate also referred to the decision reported in AIR 1973 SC 2457 in support of the contention that specific performance of contract may be granted even when damages or penalty for breach of contract is provided for in the agreement.

19. In the impugned judgment under appeal the court below decided the issue Nos. 2 and 3 in favour of the plaintiff and the other issues Nos 1, 4 and 5 against the plaintiff.

20. The finding of the court below that there was an agreement between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 to sell the suit property and the suit was not barred by limitation have not been assailed in this appeal. On consideration of the pleadings and evidence on record we also agree with the said findings. Admittedly there was an agreement by defendant No. 1 to sell the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 43,00,000.00 out of which defendant No. 1 received an advance of Taka 3,00,000.00 on 15.7.1982 on executing the deed of agreement for sale Ext I. The suit was filed on 23.1.1983 within 3 years from the date of the agreement and as such the suit was filed in time.

21. From a reading of the plaint it is apparent that the plaintiff did not deposit the transfer fee and service charge to the DIT in pursuance of memo dated 19.8.1982 issued by the DIT to the defendant No. I who sought permission from the DIT to transfer the suit property to the plaintiff in terms of the aforesaid agreement for sale dated 15.7.82.

22. Managing Director of the plaintiff as PW 1 in his deposition admitted that he could not deposit the said amounts which he was in the process of arranging. He further admitted that on 2.9.82 and 3.9.82 he saw the notices published by the defendant No. 2 in the newspaper stating that defendant No. 1 also had no right to transfer the suit property. Then he received a legal notice. He came to know that the defendant No. 2 filed TS No. 417 and obtained an order of ad interim injunction. Defendant No. 1 did not do anything for him due to the said order of injunction. Defendant No. 1 refused to execute and register the deed in his favour in respect of the suit property in terms of the contract. He was not aware of any partnership as alleged by the defendants. Defendant No. 1 is the owner of the suit property. Name of defendant No. 1 was mutated in the records of DIT. He was agreeable to get the deed registered on payment of the balance amount in terms of the contract. In cross examination he admitted that he did not send any legal notice to the defendant No. 1 to execute and register the deed on receiving the balance amount. But he asserted that within two weeks of receipt of the legal notice Ext. 6 the defendant No. 1 told him that he would not be able to execute the deed in his favour.

23. On the other hand defendant No. 1 in his written statement asserted that the plaintiff instigated defendant No. 2 to publish notices in the newspaper and to issue legal notice to the plaintiff to avoid depositing transfer fee and service charge to the DIT as he was short of fund to delay the matter and the plaintiff also got Title Suit No. 417/1982 filed through defendant No. 2 against defendant No. 1 and others and obtained order of injunction in that suit and the plaintiff had not the means to pay the price of the suit property and the defendant No. 1 never refused his obligations under the contract.

24. The defendant No. 1 as DW 1 in his deposition stated that he handed over the letter of DIT immediately after receiving the same to the plaintiff and requested him to deposit the money as soon as possible but the plaintiff did not deposit the amount. The plaintiff did not pay him the balance amount within three months in terms of the contract. Plaintiff did not pay the amount as he had no capacity to pay the same. The plaintiff did not give him any notice before filing the suit. He performed his part of the obligations in terms of the agreement for sale. But the plaintiff did not perform his obligations under the contract. He suffered loss due to the failure of the plaintiff to perform his obligations. He would have executed the deed had the plaintiff paid him money in time in terms of the contract. The plaintiff asserted in paragraph No. 22 of the plaint that the defendant refused enforcers of the contract on 2.1.1983. But we find from cross examination of PW 1 that defendant No. 1 refused to execute the deed in his favour within 2 weeks of receipt of the legal notice dated 4.9.82 (Ext. 6). There is no corroboration of the assertion of the plaintiff which has been denied by the defendant No. 1. Rather plaintiff failed to support his assertion in the plaint in his deposition and contradicted his plaint assertion that deft No. 1 refused to execute the deed on 2.1.1983. There is neither any assertion nor any evidence from plaintiffs side that he offered the balance amount to the defendant No. 1 and demanded execution and registration of the deed.

<u>25. From the above discussion we are of the view that the plaintiff failed to prove that he made any demand to the defendant No. 1 to execute the deed or that he offered the balance amount to defendant No. 1 or that the defendant No. 1 refused to execute the deed. Rather it is clear that the plaintiff without depositing the transfer fee etc. to the DIT and without offering the balance amount to the defendant No. 1 and without demanding from the defendant No. 1 amicable execution and registration of the sale deed filed the suit for specific performance of the contract with prayer for declaration that defendant No. 2 and 4 have no title in the suit property faced with newspaper notices and legal notice by defendant No. 2 and also the filing of TS No. 417 of 1982 by the defendant No. 2 and order of injunction in the suit. In these circumstances, even if it is found that defendant No. 1 has got clear title in the suit property the plaintiff is not entitled to specific performance due to his latches and default in performing his part of the obligations when there is no default of the defendant No. 1.</u>

26. Now we are to see whether the Court below was justified in refusing specific performance of the contract for sale between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1, when it found that there was a contract between the parties mainly on the ground that there is dispute over the title of the suit property between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the suit in the present form is not maintainable.

27. PW 1 stated in his deposition that he was not aware of any partnership as claimed by the defendant party. Defendant No. 1 is the owner of the suit property. Name of defendant No. 1 was mutated in the records of DIT yet in support of this the plaintiff has not produced any paper showing mutation of the name of defendant No. 1 in the record of DIT except the letter dated 19.8.82 written by Estate officer DIT to defendant No. 1 Ext. 4 another copy of which was filed by DIT and marked as Ext 3(Niya). On an examination of these two letters it is seen that the said letter addressed to M/s Hakim Humayun and Co and then the address was changed in a different type and is addressed to Mr. Abdul Hakim (Proprietor). We have seen the alen documents filed by the plaintiff. The original lease deed Ext 2 shows that suit land was leased out by DIT to M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works. The original sale deed Ext 3 shows that suit land was sold by M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works to M/S Hakim Humayun and Co and not to any proprietor such as Mr. Hakim. Deed of agreement for sale Ext. I however shows that defendant No. 1 as proprietor of M/s Hakim Humayun and Co executed the said agreement for sale in favour of the plaintiff.

28. DW 1 stated in his deposition that his father was proprietor of M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works and after taking lease of the suit plot from DIT mutated his name. His father sold the said land to him as proprietor of M/s Hakim Hymayun and Co and defendant No. 2 has no connection with that. He does not know of any partnership under the name of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. After purchase he got his name mutated with DIT and obtained sanction for constructing a ten storied building on that plot. He was an importer since 1976. But none of the documents filed by the defendant No. 1 shows that he was not sole proprietor of M/S Hakim Humayun and Co. Certificate dated 10.11.76 issued by the Chief Controller of Imports and Export in favour of defendant No. 1 (Ext. Ka) also does not show that defendant No. 1 was sole proprietor of M/S. Hakim Humayun and Co. His other statements that he obtained a sanction for construction of building from DIT has not also been supported by production of any document by him. Rather we find from the recital of the sale deed dated 27.6.73 (Ext. 3) in favour of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co that the vendor of the said deed, M/s Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works made construction of a partly incomplete one storied building in the suit plot as per commercial building plan passed by the DIT.

29. We have gone through all the documents filed by DIT and it appears therefrom that Abdul Kadir Mia signed his name as proprietor of M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works in the application dated 16.3.62 (Ext. 3Ka) submitted by him to DIT for allotment of a plot of land. Similarly in the application dated 20.7.82 (Ext. 3 Jha) Abdul Hakim signed his name as sole proprietor of M/s. Hakim Humayun and Co. On the other hand in the application dated 8.7.70 (Ext. 3 Gha) Abdul Kader Mia signed his name as managing partner of M/S Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works. But in the ocher-documents produced by DIT neither Abdul Kader signed as proprietor of M/s. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works nor Abdul Hakim as proprietor of M/S Hakim Humayun and Co.

30. DW 1 in cross-examination admitted that his father and brothers signed the plaint of TS No. 771/79 and in 'D' schedule of that plaint the suit land was shown and M/s Hakim Humayun and Co. was defendant No. 5 in that suit and was shown as a partnership company. He was not aware of any deed of settlement dated 7.10.81 amongst members of his family and denied to have signed that deed. He did not remember GIR number of his income Tax file. He did not file any bank account. He did not file any receipts of construction of one storied building. He paid Tk. 1,25,000.00 to his father but did not file any receipt. He admitted to have received Tk. 3,00,000.00 as advance from plaintiff but denied that in collusion with the plaintiff he got the suit filed.

31. From the deed of partnership (Ext 2Ka) dated 22.10.56 it is seen that M/S. Vikrampur Jahangir Metal Works was a partnership firm of four brothers and the same was registered with the Registrar of Firms on 10.1.62 vide Ext. 2 Kha which shows A. Kadir, A. Wahed, Amin Mia and Mohan Mia as four partners. Deed of Partnership dated 31.3.77 registered on 25.4.77 (Ext 2 Ga) shows that M/s Hakim Humayun and Co was a partnership firm and A Kadir and A Wahecd were the partners. Certified copy of intimation for recording changes in the constitution of the firm Ext. 2 Uma shows that M/S Hakim Humayun and Co. was registered under registration No. PF/21402 dated 13.4.76 and out of five partners Mrs. Azimun, Azizul Hoque and Md. Abdul Hakim retired with effect from 31.3.77 and the said firm was reconstituted with A Kadir Mia and Abdul Wahid Mia. Certified copy of the plaint of TS 771/79 (Ext 2 Chha) shows that A Kadir, A Hakim, Azizul Hoque and Tofazzal Miah filed the suit against Abdul Wahid, Md. Humayun, Md. Ali Akbar, Md. Maqsud Mia, M/S Hakim Humayun and Co. a partnership firm and M/S. VIP Corner, another partnership firm for partition of ejmali properties and business and also for accounts showing the suit property in the 'D' schedule and admitting that M/S Hakim Humayun and Co was a partnership firm with A. Kadir and A Wahid as two partners having eight annas share each and the said firm purchased the suit land and constructed one storied building with ten storied foundation after purchase and delivery of possession in its favour. Deed of family settlement dated 7.10.81 shows that Abdul Washed Mia and his sons and Abdul Kader Mia and his sons executed the said family settlement deed admitting therein that the suit property at Motijheel (described in 'G' schedule of the deed) belonged to Abdul Kadir and Abdul Wahid in equal eight annas share each and they will remain in joint possession. Certified copy of the petition dated 8.7.84 Ext Ga shows that defendant Nos. 1-4 of TS 771/79 filed the application for transposing them as plaintiff Nos 1-4 and to transpose the plaintiff Nos. 1-4 as defendant Nos. 1-4 as they fraudulently filed an application earlier for withdrawal of the suit. Certified copy of the order dated 19.12.84 Ext Uma shows that prayer for transposition in TS 771/79 was allowed and suit fixed on 17.1.85 for peremptory hearing with TS 133/1984 which came to that court on transfer under order of the learned District Judge. Learned Advocate of the parties admitted that TS 417 of 1982 on transfer was renumbered as TS 133/1984. But no copy of the alleged petition of compromise or petition for withdrawal of TS 771/74 were filed by either of the parties to show what were the averments made in these petitions.

<u>32. From the aforesaid discussion it is very clear that there is serious dispute between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 over the title of the suit property. We find nothing to disagree with the firm finding of the Court below that there is dispute between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 over the title of the suit property and the matter is subjudice in other suits and it is not in accordance with law to decide the dispute of title over the suit land between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the present suit framed in the present form.</u>

33. The learned Advocate for the appellant referred to the case of Madduria Chetty Vs. Babu Saheb, reported in 52 IC 971 in support of his contention that dispute of title can be decided in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land. But it appears from the aforesaid decision that the vendors insisted on the purchasers to complete the contract for sale within a given time by paying the balance of the consideration without clearing an earlier mortgage of the suit property was demanded by the purchasers to clear the title and the vendors rescinded' the contract and sued for recession of the contract and the purchasers on the other hand sued for specific performance of the contract. Both the suits were decided in favour of the purchasers. It was held "A purchaser is entitled to a good and marketable title. If the title is found to be doubtful so as to require investigation he can not be compelled either to rescind the contract or to accept without investigation of the doubtful title. The purchasers were entitled to sue for specific performance and an enquiry into title. The evidence in this case established title to their satisfaction." In our opinion facts of that case are distinguishable. Enquiry in that case was limited between the parties to the contract as to the subsistence of a mortgage which the purchasers could claim to be cleared under section 18(c) of the Specific Relief Act in a suit for specific performance of contract. The facts of the case reported in AIR 26 Mad 597; AIR 1961 Raj 196 and AIR 1973 SC 2457 are clearly distinguishable and the principles laid down in those cases are not applicable in the present case. On the other hand in the case of Govinda Vs. Apathsahaya reported in AIR 1915 Mad 305 the defendant entered into a contract to sell the property in which he has only half share and the plaintiff sued for specific performance of the contract to sell the entire land. The prayer for specific performance was refused with the observation: "Execution of the sale deed by the defendant, over property which does not belong to him, would be an improper act in itself as it is calculated to throw a cloud over the title of his brother, which would be sufficient to give him a cause of action for a declaratory suit."

34. We have already found that there is serious dispute between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 over the title of the suit property. The plaintiff and defendant No. 1 failed to prove satisfactorily possession of deft. No. 1 in the suit property by adducing independent and trustworthy evidence in the face of the evidence adduced by the defendant No. 2 in support of his possession corroborated by the evidence of DW 3 and DW 4 and admission of defendant No. 1 in the plaint of TS No. 771 of 1979 and deed of family settlement dated 7.10.81. In such circumstances we are of the view that the plaintiff is not entitled to specific performance of the contract for sale of the suit property when title and possession therein of the defendant No. 1 contracting to sell the same is disputed. Complicated question of title and possession of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property can not be decided in the present suit for specific performance of contract for sale of the suit land. We are of the view that there is no scope for deciding the question of title of the defendant No. 1 in this suit for specific performance of contract by the buyer or to declare that the defendant Nos. 2 & 3 have no title in the suit property. Specific performance being an equitable relief the Court is not bound to grant the same merely because the contract between plaintiff and defendant No. 1 has been proved to the prejudice of other defendants who arc not parties to the said contract.

35. In the case of Nowab Meah Vs. Ezazuddin Ahmed reported in 13 DLR 554 the court refused specific performance of the contract on a finding that defendant Nos. 3 and 4 were not parties to the contract holding "To grant specific performance of contract is absolutely within the discretion of the court and no rigid rule can be laid down when and where this discretion can be exercised by the Court. The discretion that shall have to be exercised by the Court will depend on the circumstances of each case but that discretion must be a judicial one".

<u>36. In the case of Administrator of Wakfs Vs. Mst. Sahere Khatun, reported in 28 DLR 238 the Court refused specific performance of the contract holding. "It is doubtful if the deed of sale which may be executed in pursuance of decree made in this suit will confer any clear title upon the plaintiff. It is no doubt true that ordinarily the object of enforcement of an agreement for sale is the concern of the purchaser, but we can not shut our eyes to the distinct possibility that in consequence of a decree passed in this suit, the parties may be involved in further litigation on the question as to whether the Mutawall is did lawfully transfer the properties. The discretionary power of the Court to refuse specific performance of contract should be exercised in our opinion in this case on these grounds also."</u>

37. Agreeing with the views expressed in the aforesaid decisions we hold that that the court below rightly refused to exercise the discretion in favour of the plaintiff.

38. Moreover in this case the plaintiff also failed to prove that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract and that the defendant No. 1 failed to perform his part of the contract and there was refusal on the part of the defendant No. 1 to execute and register the sale deed in pursuance of the contract. There is substance in the contention of the defendant No. 1 that the plaintiff was not in a position to pay the transfer fee and service charge to the DIT in terms of the agreement for sale and he also failed to offer to deft No. 1 the balance sum of Taka 40,00,000.00 and he filed the suit to buy time without asking him to amicably execute and register the sale deed or to clear the dispute of title to the suit property. Such conduct disentitled the plaintiff to an equitable relief. Had the plaintiff opted to take the conveyance inspire of the claim of the defendant No. 2 from the defendant No. 1 his prayer for specific performance on the refusal of the deft. No. 1 on proof of his ready and willingness could be considered. But in the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the plaintiff is not entitled to specific performance of contract even if he abandons the prayer for declaration sought for in this suit for the simple reason that interest of non-contracting parties who are not bound by the contract should not be affected by the decree.

<u>39. Learned Advocate for the appellant referred to the case of Pitchayya Vs. Venkataramayya reported in AIR 1943 Mad 497 which is a single bench decision in support of his contention that prayer for declaration by the purchaser in a suit for specific performance of contract was maintainable. In that reported case the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance against the heirs of the vendor and an ostensible transferee from the vendor with prayer for declaration that the sale deed by the vendor in favour of the said transferee was a nominal transaction. It was held that prayer for declaration was maintainable. But the facts of the case before us is just the reverse. Here the defendant No. 2 who has not entered into the contract alleged that the transfer in favour of defendant No. 1 was a mere nominal transaction. Moreover under section 27(c) of the Specific Relief Act the purchaser was entitled to such a declaration in a suit for specific performance. That decision is not applicable in the present case. We agree with the court below that plaintiff's prayer for declaration that defendant Nos. 2 and 4 have no title in the suit property in the suit for specific performance of contract by the purchaser was not maintainable since the plaintiff acquired no interest in the suit property under the contract for sale.</u>

40. We also find no substance in the submission that the specific performance of the contract against the defendant No. 1 who is alleged to be benamdar of defendant No. 2 should be allowed when the contract has been proved since a benamdar is permitted to transfer under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and remedy of the defendant No. 2, the alleged real owner lies in a separate suit contemplated under that section. In our view the provision of that section is not applicable in this case.

<u>41. The plaintiff admittedly paid the sum of Taka 3,00,000.00 to the defendant No. 1 as earnest money. Though the plaintiff has not specifically prayed for refund of the amount, under the residuary prayer in the plaint (for other reliefs to which the plaintiff is found entitled) a decree for refund of the earnest money in our view should be allowed. The plaintiff has neither prayed for compensation in lieu of specific performance nor refund of the earnest money with interest in the plaint. But the learned Senior Advocate for the appellant submitted that since the contract and payment of earnest money has been admitted by the defendant No. 1 the plaintiff is entitled to refund of the earnest money with compensation. Under the 2nd clause of section 19 of the Specific Relief Act plaintiff is entitled to compensation when the contract was broken by the defendant in lieu of specific performance. We have already found that there was no violation of contract by the defendant No. 1. So the plaintiff is not entitled to any compensation.</u>

<u>42. In the case of Jaggo Bai Vs. Hari Har Prosad Singh reported in PLD 1947 PC 406 it has been held by the Privy Council that the plaintiff is entitled to reasonable interest on the earnest money from the date of wrongfully with-holding the sum. Only in this appeal in course of argument the appellant prayed for refund of the earnest money and it cannot be said that the defendant No. 1 has been wrongfully withholding the sum inspite of demand. So the plaintiff is not entitled to any interest up to the passing of the decree in this appeal. If the defendant No. 1 fails to refund the earnest money the plaintiff will be entitled to interest on the amount from the date of decree till realization at the rate of 15% per annum.</u>

43. In the result the appeal succeeds in part. The judgment and decree of the court below is modified and suit is decreed in part for recovery of the sum of Taka 3,00,00,000.00 by the plaintiff from the defendant No. 1 with interest at the rate of 15% per annum from the date of decree till realization. Dismissal of the suit for specific performance of the contract for sale of the suit land is hereby affirmed.

44. There will be no order as to costs in the facts and circumstances of the case. Opinion expressed in this judgment as to the title and possession of the parties will not be binding on the court below in deciding any case on merits between the defendants over the title of the suit property. In that view of the matter cross-objection filed by the respondent No. 1 is rejected.

End.
